data:
A cell is Go with statements allowed at the top level, as in a REPL:
import "strings" func words(s string) []string { return strings.Fields(s) } w := words("to be or not to be") len(w) // the final expression is shown $ notebook run words.md ── cell 0 (line 4, ran in 86µs) 6
data.declarations-and-statements#Declarations: Top-level func, type and import are declarations of the notebook. Everything else is a statement of the cell, run in order. The names a cell defines at its top level — by :=, var, const, func or type — are notebook variables: every cell, and every function, can read them.
data.errors-point-at-the-notebook#Errors poin:
The generated program carries //line directives, so compiler errors and panic stacks name the notebook’s own lines, not the generated file’s.
A cell that fails stops the cells that read it, and they say why:
```go var xs []int first := xs[0] ``` ```go first + 1 ``` $ notebook run panic.md ── cell 0 (line 4, ran in 104µs) error: panic: runtime error: index out of range [0] with length 0 … main._nbcell0(…) …/panic.md:5 +0x3c … ── cell 1 (line 9, kept) error: not run: cell 0 failed notebook: 2 cell(s) failed (The stack is shortened here; the frame of the cell names panic.md:5, the line of xs[0].)
data.no-assignment-to-another-cells-variable#:
A cell may not assign to a variable another cell defines: the dependency graph would not see the change.
```go x := 1 ``` ```go x = 2 ``` $ notebook run rules.md … error: 8:1: cell 1: cannot assign to x, which cell 0 defines; define a new name instead notebook: 1 cell(s) failed Mutation through a method or a slice element cannot be seen statically and is not refused (marimo makes the same choice).
data.one-definition-per-name#One definition p: Each notebook variable is defined by exactly one cell. Go already forbids two package-level declarations of a name, which gives this rule for free.
data.private-names-stay-in-their-cell#Private: A name starting with _, and err — which nearly every cell declares and none means to share — are local to their cell. Two cells may each have their own err.
data.the-final-expression-is-shown#The final:
A cell’s final expression statement is its display value. A call with several results (fmt.Println’s n, err) is run for its effect and not shown.
A value with a Display() map[string][]byte method (the runtime.Displayer interface) shows itself: the map goes from a MIME type — text/plain, text/html, image/svg+xml, image/png, … — to the bytes of that representation. Values without one show their %v.
What a cell prints, through os.Stdout, the println builtin or C code, is captured and shown with it. (On systems without dup2 — Windows, js, wasip1 — os.Stdout and os.Stderr are swapped instead, and println is not captured.)
data.the-three-rules#The three rules: They make the order of execution a function of the code, as in marimo, rather than of the order cells were run in.
data.variables-that-cannot-be-shared#Variable: A notebook variable becomes a package-level variable of the generated program, which needs its type to be written there. A variable whose type cannot be written outside its package (an unexported type) cannot be shared: the error says so and suggests a private name (_x).

data:
go install github.com/go-notebook/notebook/cmd/notebook@latest Usage: notebook [command] Available Commands: completion Generate the autocompletion script for the specified shell help Help about any command html Run the notebook and write its results as a page next to it (or --output) irb Start an interactive Ruby session, as irb, on the notebook's Ruby and bindings run Run the notebook and print each cell's results serve Run the notebook again every time it changes, showing it live in a browser watch Run the notebook again every time it changes, keeping its page current notebook --help lists the verbs, notebook --help the flags of one, and notebook --version the release.
Edit the .md in any editor. Every verb goes through the same kernel, so each one runs only the cells whose code or inputs changed since the last run of that notebook, whichever verb ran it (see The kernel).
data.flags#Flags:
Flag Default Verbs Meaning -o, --output .html html, watch the HTML file to write --addr 127.0.0.1:8888 serve where serve listens --interval 300ms watch, serve how often the file is looked at (must be positive) -w, --work under the user cache directory all the work directory --runtime-src all use the go-notebook source tree at this path instead of a released runtime -t, --timeout 0 (no limit) all stop a cell, in Go or in Ruby, that runs longer than this (30s, 2m): its worker is killed, the cell fails, and the next run starts a new worker; for irb, an input -m, --memory 0 (no limit) all stop a cell whose worker’s Go heap holds more than this many MiB: the garbage collector keeps under it as long as it can, then the worker is stopped and the cell fails; for irb, an input -s, --save irb write the session, at its end, as a notebook of Ruby cells --svg-dir irb save each figure an input shows as an SVG file in this directory --history go-notebook/irb_history under the user config directory irb the history file (mode 0600, the inputs only) --history-size 1000 irb how many inputs the history keeps; 0: no history file Flags are POSIX (since v0.4.0): a long name takes two dashes, a one-letter shorthand one (notebook html -o out.html nb.md, notebook run --timeout 30s nb.md), before or after the notebook. A verb refuses a flag it does not read. The single-dash spelling of v0.3 and earlier (-timeout 30s) is still accepted, with a note on stderr.
NOTEBOOK_REPLACE=module=dir,module=dir points modules of the work module at local checkouts, to run a notebook against a library being changed (for example github.com/go-scikit/ruby=../ruby for the Ruby bindings).
data.html#html: notebook html analysis.md # writes analysis.html notebook html -o report.html analysis.md Runs the notebook and writes a standalone HTML page: the prose rendered as Markdown, each code cell with what it printed, showed or failed with. The page has no scripts and no external resources, and raw HTML in the prose is left out (goldmark’s safe default), so a page made from someone else’s notebook runs nothing of theirs but what its cells chose to display.
data.irb#irb: notebook irb notebook irb --timeout 30s --memory 2048 --save session.md --svg-dir figures notebook irb < script.rb An interactive Ruby session, as irb, on the Ruby of Ruby cells (rbgo with the go-scikit bindings), with no notebook file (v0.5.0 and later): => inspect after each input, _ the last value, exceptions shown without ending the session, reassignment allowed, multi-line input, a line editor with history and Tab completion. Each input runs in a worker process, to which --timeout and --memory apply; --save writes the session as a notebook that notebook run runs. The irb page has the details.
data.run#run:
notebook run analysis.md Runs the notebook and prints each code cell: its index, its line in the file, and either how long it ran or kept when its result was kept from before; then what it printed, what it showed and its error, indented.
$ notebook run spectrum.md ── cell 0 (line 4, kept) ── cell 1 (line 12, kept) ── cell 2 (line 19, ran in 42µs) 9.54929284535666e-07 The exit status is non-zero when a cell failed (notebook: 1 cell(s) failed), so notebook run can gate a CI job.
data.serve#serve:
notebook serve analysis.md notebook serve --addr 127.0.0.1:9000 analysis.md The same loop as watch, but the page is served at --addr (default 127.0.0.1:8888) instead of written to a file:
$ notebook serve spectrum.md serving spectrum.md at http://127.0.0.1:8888/ 21:28:21 0 of 3 cells ran, build 252ms: ok The page reloads itself through a server-sent event when the results change, and keeps its scroll position. A notebook that cannot run at all (for example, an import that cannot be fetched) is shown as an error page instead of a stale one. The served page is the html page plus the small script that reloads it.
data.the-runtime-the-notebook-links#The runti: The compiled notebook links package runtime of go-notebook. A notebook installed from a release tag makes the notebook’s work module require that same release. A notebook built from a source checkout uses that checkout instead (through a replace directive), since its pseudo-version names no published runtime with the same code; --runtime-src points at a checkout explicitly.
data.the-work-directory#The work directory: By default each notebook has its own work directory under the user’s cache directory (go-notebook/
data.watch#watch:
notebook watch analysis.md Runs the notebook every time the file changes, and keeps analysis.html (or -o/--output) current. Each run prints one line:
21:28:21 0 of 3 cells ran, build 252ms: ok It looks at the file’s modification time every --interval (300 ms by default), and runs until interrupted.

data: Mirrored from docs/design.md in go-notebook/notebook at main 1cc66fc. Everything from the first section on is that file, verbatim.
data.a-cell-is-go-with-top-level-statements#A:
import "math" func sq(x float64) float64 { return x * x } y := sq(math.Pi) y Top-level func, type and import are declarations of the notebook. The rest is the cell’s statements, run in order. The names a cell defines at the top level (:=, var, const, func, type) are notebook variables, readable from every cell. A final expression is the cell’s display value; a call with several results (fmt.Println’s n, err) is run for its effect and not shown.
Three rules make the order a function of the code, as in marimo:
One definition per name. Go already forbids two package-level declarations of a name, which gives this rule for free. No assignment to another cell’s variable. The dependency graph would not see the change. Mutation through a method or an element cannot be seen statically and is not refused (marimo makes the same choice). Private names stay in their cell: a name starting with _, and err, which nearly every cell declares and none means to share.
data.a-notebook-is-a-markdown-file#A notebook:
Its ```go blocks are the cells; everything else is prose, kept byte for byte (format.Parse(src).String() == src for every input; it is fuzzed). GitHub and every Markdown viewer show a notebook as a document, and a diff of a notebook is a diff of text. No output is ever written into it.
A valid Go file was considered first and rejected. Go allows no statements at the top level, and x := load(path) or fmt.Println(x) at the top level of a cell is most of what a notebook is. Wrapping every cell in a function costs the user more than editor support on the raw file gains. The kernel produces the valid Go program instead; see below.
data.dependencies-come-from-syntax-types-come:
analysis finds each cell’s definitions and free identifiers from the parse alone, so it works on code that does not compile yet. Those give the graph, its order and its errors (cycles, double definitions, foreign assignments).
gen writes the program. Each cell becomes a function. Its variables become package-level variables, which needs their types: gen type-checks the cells one by one in dependency order to learn them. The cells’ text is kept as it is and edited in place: := becomes = , var x T becomes x = *new(T) so that running the cell again resets it, constants move to package level, and the display value is wrapped in _k.Show(...). /*line nb.md:L:C*/ directives point every line back into the notebook, so compiler errors and panic stacks name the notebook’s own lines.
A variable whose type cannot be written outside its package (an unexported type) cannot be shared. The error says so and suggests a private name.
data.display#Display: runtime.Displayer is a MIME bundle: Display() map[string][]byte with text/plain, text/html, image/svg+xml, image/png… Values without one show their %v.
data.native-code-kept-values#Native code, kep:
The kernel compiles the program into a worker process. Go’s build cache makes rebuilding after a one-cell edit cost about a tenth of a second here. The kernel then does the least work that brings the results up to date:
A cell’s key is a hash of its source, the import paths of the packages it refers to, the Go toolchain’s version, the work module’s go.sum when the cell uses a package outside the standard library, and the keys of the cells it reads. Its position is not part of it, so moving cells runs nothing; neither does an import another cell adds. Upgrading Go, or a dependency, runs again what it could change. An unchanged key keeps its result. After a rebuild, the variables the cell made are handed to the new worker, not computed again. Values are encoded with their own MarshalBinary when they have one, and with gob when every field they can hold is exported (gob would silently drop the others). Anything else is volatile: its cell runs again, but only when a cell that reads it has to run. Results and values are kept on disk in the work directory, so a new kernel, or the next notebook run, starts where the last one stopped. A failing cell stops its readers, which report why. A worker that dies (os.Exit, a crash outside the recovered call) is restarted on the next run. This assumes a cell computes the same values from the same inputs. A cell that reads the clock or an unseeded generator should be run explicitly (Kernel.RunCell).
data.not-yet#Not yet: A Jupyter wire-protocol front end (JupyterLab, VS Code), and a go-widgets native and wasm UI. Running independent branches of the graph concurrently. Real LaTeX in prose through go-tex; for now $...$ stays as text. MarshalBinary on go-ndarray arrays, so that arrays are kept rather than volatile.
data.output-capture#Output capture: What a cell prints, through os.Stdout, the println builtin or C code, is captured by pointing file descriptors 1 and 2 at a pipe for the duration of the cell. The protocol replies travel on a duplicate of the original standard output, so a cell can never forge one. Systems without dup2 (Windows, js, wasip1) swap os.Stdout and os.Stderr instead, and do not capture println.
data.what-exists-and-what-each-gets-wrong#Wha: execution state between cells order speed Jupyter (Python) interpreter, one process values, hidden and mutable whatever order the cells were clicked in interpreted; numpy in C gophernotes gomacro interpreter values clicked order interpreted Go; generics partial GoNB compiles the cell plus the declarations it memorised, then runs it declarations only — values are computed again on every run (it ships a cache package as the workaround) clicked order native marimo (Python) interpreter values reactive graph from static analysis; one definition per name interpreted None has native speed, kept values and a reproducible order together. go-notebook is built to have all three.

data:
notebook irb (go-notebook v0.5.0 and later) is an interactive Ruby session, as Ruby’s irb, on the Ruby that runs Ruby cells: rbgo with the go-scikit bindings — Stats, Special, Optimize, Integrate, DataFrame, Plot and NDArray. There is no notebook file: inputs are typed, evaluated and shown one at a time.
$ notebook irb irb(main):001> x = [2.1, 3.4, 1.9, 5.6] => [2.1, 3.4, 1.9, 5.6] irb(main):002> fit = Stats::Normal.fit(x) => # irb(main):003> fit.loc => 3.25 irb(main):004> _ * 2 => 6.5 irb(main):005> def sq(v) irb(main):006* v * v irb(main):007* end => :sq irb(main):008> sq(3) => 9 irb(main):009> x = x.sum => 13.0 irb(main):010> raise "boom" boom (RuntimeError) from (irb):10:in '' irb(main):011> s = "multi irb(main):012" line string" => "multi\nline string" irb(main):013> exit (A real transcript, from notebook irb < session.rb: when standard input is not a terminal, each line is echoed after its prompt.)
The first session builds the worker program, once (building the Ruby worker; it fetches and compiles rbgo the first time); later sessions start at once. It needs the Go toolchain, as notebook run does.
data.figures#Figures:
A value that shows itself — a Plot figure — is never printed as SVG:
irb(main):014> fig, ax = Plot.subplots => [#, #] irb(main):015> ax.plot([1, 2, 3], [3, 1, 2]) => nil irb(main):016> fig => # (a figure: --svg-dir saves it as SVG) With --svg-dir figures, each figure an input shows is written to figures/figure-N.svg, and the line says where.
data.flags#Flags: Flag Default Meaning -t, --timeout 0 (no limit) stop an input that runs longer than this -m, --memory 0 (no limit) stop an input whose worker holds more than this many MiB of Go heap -s, --save write the session, at its end, as a notebook --svg-dir save each figure as an SVG file in this directory --history see above the history file --history-size 1000 how many inputs the history keeps; 0: no history file -w, --work go-notebook/irb under the user cache directory where the worker is built --runtime-src use the go-notebook source tree at this path instead of a released runtime NOTEBOOK_REPLACE points modules of the worker’s module at local checkouts, as for a notebook (see the command).
data.history#History:
The inputs are kept in irb_history under the user config directory’s go-notebook (~/.config/go-notebook/irb_history on Linux, ~/Library/Application Support/go-notebook/irb_history on macOS, %AppData%\go-notebook\irb_history on Windows), in irb’s format (a multi-line input’s lines joined by \):
the inputs only, never their values; the last --history-size of them (1000, irb’s default; 0 keeps no file); mode 0600 (read and written by its owner only), in a directory made with mode 0700; it is written through a new file renamed over the old one, and another session’s inputs saved meanwhile are kept; a file that cannot be read, or one over 8 MiB, is left alone, and the session keeps no history.
data.limits-each-input-in-a-worker#Limits: ea:
The interpreter runs in a worker process, as a notebook’s cells do, and --timeout and --memory apply to each input:
$ notebook irb --timeout 3s --memory 256 irb(main):001> kept = 1 => 1 irb(main):002> loop { } stopped: the input ran longer than 3s, the limit; its worker was killed notebook irb: the session's state (locals, methods, classes) is lost; the next input starts a new worker irb(main):003> kept undefined local variable or method 'kept' for main (NameError) from (irb):3:in '' rbgo cannot be interrupted in the middle of an evaluation, so stopping an input — a limit, or Ctrl-C — kills its worker: the prompt stays, the next input gets a new worker, and the session says that the old one’s locals, methods and classes are gone. The worker is in a process group of its own, so Ctrl-C in the terminal reaches the session, which stops the worker; it is not the worker that dies of it.
The worker’s standard input is empty (gets returns nil): its own is the protocol with the session.
data.not-in-it#Not in it: Go cells: a session is Ruby only. irb’s own commands beyond exit and quit (ls, show_source, edit, …), pp and inspect modes, and colour are not there yet.
data.saving-the-session-as-a-notebook#Saving:
--save session.md writes, when the session ends, the inputs that ran as ```ruby cells, which notebook run session.md runs again. A notebook has rules a session does not — each name is defined by one cell, and _ stays in its cell — so the inputs are grouped:
one cell per input, by default; an input that defines or assigns a name an earlier cell defines (x = x.sum after x = [...], a method defined again) is joined to that cell, with every input in between; an input that reads _ is joined to the one before it, which then assigns _ its value (_ = begin … end), as irb did; should the result still break a rule (two methods that call each other, defined in two inputs), all the inputs make one cell. The inputs that raised an exception are left out, and the notebook says how many. For the session above:
```ruby x = [2.1, 3.4, 1.9, 5.6] fit = Stats::Normal.fit(x) _ = begin fit.loc end _ * 2 def sq(v) v * v end sq(3) x = x.sum ``` ```ruby s = "multi line string" ``` The saved notebook is a record of what ran, not of the session’s state: a worker stopped in the middle of the session does not change it.
data.the-line-editor#The line editor:
On a terminal, lines are edited with go-ruby-reline, a pure-Go port of Ruby’s Reline, through its terminal package — on Linux, macOS and Windows 10 and later:
emacs keys (Ctrl-A/E/K/U/W/Y, Alt-F/B, …), the arrow, Home, End and Delete keys, undo; history with Up and Down, and Ctrl-R to search it; a multi-line input comes back whole; bracketed paste: a pasted block is inserted as it is, newlines included; Tab completion of locals, methods of main, keywords, constants and the bindings (St → Stats, Stats::Nor → Stats::Normal), and of the methods of a variable’s value or a constant path’s (x.so → x.sort, Stats::Normal.fi → Stats::Normal.fit), as IRB’s default completor does. A word is completed by asking the worker about the names it holds: completion never evaluates an expression the word contains (xs.first.ti completes to nothing), so pressing Tab runs none of your code. A completion that takes more than five seconds (a methods method that does not return) stops the worker, and the next input says so. When standard input is not a terminal, lines are read as they come, with no editing, and echoed after their prompt, so notebook irb < script.rb prints a transcript and a session can be scripted and tested.
data.what-it-does-as-irb-does#What it does as: Results => and the value’s inspect after each input; _ is the last value Exceptions message (Class) and the frames in the session (twelve at most); the session goes on, and _ keeps the last value that was not one Reassignment any local may be assigned again: there is no dependency graph here, unlike in a notebook Multi-line input an input that is not finished — an open def, do, bracket, string, heredoc, or a line ending in an operator or \ — continues on the next line, under irb’s continuation prompt (*, or the quote of an open string) Ending exit, quit, exit! or Ctrl-D; Ruby’s exit inside an input ends it too Ctrl-C abandons the line being typed; during an input, stops it (see below) Whether an input is finished is decided by rbgo’s own parser (go-ruby-parser): an input it finds ending in the middle of a construct continues. Where the parser accepts an unterminated literal as it is (a string, a heredoc, a regexp, =begin), the port of IRB’s lexer in go-ruby-irb says it is open. Any other syntax error is evaluated, for Ruby to report.

data: Each run takes the notebook’s current code cells and does the least work that brings every result up to date. Four steps get there: the analysis of the cells, the generated program, the cell keys, and the value store.
data.a-cells-key#A cell’s key:
A cell’s key is a hash of:
its source; the import paths of the packages it refers to; the Go toolchain’s version; the work module’s go.sum, when the cell uses a package outside the standard library (any module could be behind such a package, transitively, so the whole go.sum is the honest summary); the keys of the cells it reads. Its position is not part of the key, so moving cells runs nothing; neither does an import another cell adds. Upgrading Go, or a dependency, runs again what it could change, and only that: a cell using only the standard library is not run again by a go.sum change. Because a key includes the keys of its inputs, a change propagates to exactly the cells downstream of it.
data.kept-values#Kept values:
To hand a value over, or to keep it on disk, the kernel encodes it:
with its own MarshalBinary when it has one; with gob when every field it can hold is exported (gob would silently drop the others). Anything else — a func, a channel, unexported state — is volatile: its cell runs again, but only when a cell that reads it has to run.
data.on-disk#On disk: Results and values are kept in the work directory, so a new kernel, or the next notebook run, starts where the last one stopped. The notebook command gives each notebook its own work directory under the user’s cache directory.
data.the-assumption#The assumption: All of this assumes a cell computes the same values from the same inputs. A cell that reads the clock or an unseeded random generator does not; such a cell should be run explicitly — Kernel.RunCell runs a cell again even if nothing changed, together with every cell that reads it.
data.the-dependency-graph#The dependency grap:
Package analysis finds each cell’s definitions and free identifiers from the parse alone. It needs no type information, so it works on code that does not compile yet.
A cell depends on the cells that define the names it reads. That gives the graph, the order of execution, and the static errors: cycles, double definitions and assignments to another cell’s variable (see Cells). The order is therefore a function of the code, never of the order cells were run in or appear in.
data.the-generated-program#The generated prog:
Package gen writes the Go program the kernel compiles:
each cell becomes a function; its variables become package-level variables, so every cell can read them and their values outlive the call. That needs their types, so gen type-checks the cells one by one, in dependency order, with go/types; the cells’ text is kept as it is and edited in place: := becomes = , var x T becomes x = *new(T) (so running the cell again resets it), constants move to package level, and the display value is wrapped in a call that shows it; //line nb.md:L:C directives point every line back into the notebook. The kernel compiles this program into a worker process and drives it through package runtime: one JSON request per line on the worker’s standard input (run, get, set, exit) and one reply per line on its standard output. What a cell prints goes to a pipe of its own, so it can never be mistaken for a reply.
Go’s build cache makes rebuilding after a one-cell edit cost about a tenth of a second.
data.using-the-kernel-from-go#Using the kerne: k, err := kernel.New(kernel.Options{Dir: work, Name: "analysis.md"}) if err != nil { … } defer k.Close() rep, err := k.Run(cells) // cells: []gen.Code{{Source: …, Line: …}, …} for _, r := range rep.Results { // r.Ran, r.Took, r.Output, r.Display, r.Error } Report.Built says whether the worker was rebuilt, Report.Build how long generating and building took, and Report.Diags holds the static errors.
data.what-runs#What runs:
A cell whose key… … did not change keeps its result and is not run changed runs, and so does every cell whose key changes because of it did not change, but made a volatile value that a running cell reads runs again, to make that value (see below) reads a cell that failed is not run, and reports not run: cell N failed When the program changes, the worker is rebuilt and restarted. The variables made by unchanged cells are handed to the new worker instead of being computed again.
A worker that dies (os.Exit, a crash outside the recovered call) is restarted on the next run.

data:
A notebook is a Markdown file. Its fenced code blocks whose info string’s first word is go are code cells; everything between them is prose, kept byte for byte.
# Spectrum Some prose, with a list, a table, a link: any Markdown. ```go x := 40 + 2 ``` ```python # A block in another language is prose, not a cell. ```
data.fences#Fences: Fences follow CommonMark: three or more backticks or tildes, indented by at most three spaces, closed by a fence of the same character at least as long. A code block in another language is prose.
data.nothing-is-written-back#Nothing is writt:
No output is ever stored in the file. Results live in the kernel’s value store (see The kernel) and in exports such as the HTML page written by notebook html.
Because of that:
GitHub, and every Markdown viewer, shows a notebook as a document; a diff of a notebook is a diff of text, with no execution counts or outputs; reading and writing a notebook round-trips exactly: format.Parse(src).String() == src for every input, and that property is fuzzed.
data.the-packages#The packages: The Markdown is read and written by package format. Its Parse returns a Notebook whose Cells are either code or prose, each with its line in the file.
data.why-not-a-valid-go-file#Why not a valid: A .go file was considered first and rejected. Go allows no statements at the top level, and x := load(path) or fmt.Println(x) at the top level of a cell is most of what a notebook is. Wrapping every cell in a function costs the user more than editor support on the raw file gains. The kernel produces the valid Go program instead: see The kernel.

data:
A ```ruby block is a Ruby cell (go-notebook v0.3.0 and later). The Ruby is rbgo, a Ruby bytecode VM written in Go, with the go-scikit bindings registered over the same Go libraries a Go cell imports:
Ruby Go library Counterpart Stats go-statistics/stats scipy.stats Special go-numerics/special scipy.special Optimize go-numerics/optimize scipy.optimize Integrate go-numerics/integrate scipy.integrate DataFrame go-dataframe/dataframe pandas Plot go-plot/plot matplotlib.pyplot NDArray go-ndarray/ndarray (rbgo’s own) numpy.ndarray Every binding calls the Go function it is named after; the bindings’ README lists every name.
The kernel adds github.com/go-scikit/ruby to the notebook’s work module by itself, and builds the worker with -tags rbgo_core (the Ruby language and its numeric stack, without gems). A notebook needs nothing more than go-notebook.
To try the same Ruby line by line, as irb, without a notebook file, run notebook irb.
data.a-mixed-notebook#A mixed notebook:
A Go cell makes the data, a Ruby cell fits it with a go-scikit binding, and a Go cell reads the fit back (the file’s prose is left out here):
```go xs := []float64{2.1, 3.4, 1.9, 5.6, 4.4, 3.3, 2.8, 4.9} ``` ```ruby fit = Stats::Normal.fit(xs) loc, scale = fit.loc, fit.scale ks = Stats.ks_1samp(xs) { |x| fit.cdf(x) } pvalue = ks.pvalue fit ``` ```go import "fmt" fmt.Printf("loc %.4f, scale %.4f, KS p-value %.4f\n", loc, scale, pvalue) ``` In a module whose go.mod has tool github.com/go-notebook/notebook/cmd/notebook and requires github.com/go-notebook/notebook v0.3.0:
$ go tool notebook run first.md ── cell 0 (line 6, ran in 0s) ── cell 1 (line 13, ran in 366µs) # ── cell 2 (line 23, ran in 3µs) loc 3.5500, scale 1.2359, KS p-value 0.9381 In the Ruby cell xs is an Array of Floats; in the last Go cell loc, scale and pvalue are float64s. (A real transcript, from go-notebook v0.3.0 with go-scikit/ruby v0.1.0; the line numbers are those of the full file.) A larger example, with an NDArray and a plot, is examples/mixed.md.
data.how-values-cross-between-go-and-ruby#How:
Only variables cross. A Go cell sees a Ruby cell’s top-level locals, not its methods, constants or classes, nor a local named like a Go keyword or predeclared identifier (len, type, int). A Ruby cell sees a Go cell’s variables, not its funcs or types.
Go to Ruby. Before a Ruby cell runs, each Go variable it reads becomes a Ruby local of the same name (a constant when the name starts with an upper-case letter):
numbers, strings and booleans as such; slices as Arrays, maps as Hashes; an *ndarray.Array as the NDArray itself, not a copy; any other value (a *plot.Figure, a struct) as an object that comes back to Go as itself. Ruby to Go. After a Ruby cell runs, each local it assigns becomes a Go variable whose type is the type of its value:
Ruby value Go type nil any (nil) true, false bool Integer int64 (*big.Int when it does not fit) Float float64 String string Symbol ruby.Symbol Complex complex128 Rational *big.Rat NDArray *ndarray.Array, the same array Array of all Floats, all Integers, all Strings, all booleans []float64, []int64, []string, []bool any other Array []any Hash with String keys map[string]any Hash with Symbol keys map[ruby.Symbol]any any other Hash map[any]any a go-scikit object the Go value it wraps: *plot.Figure, stats.TTestResult, *optimize.Result, … any other Ruby object ruby.Value, which a Go cell can Call The type comes from the value, so it is known once the Ruby cell has run. A Go cell that reads a Ruby variable whose type is not known yet waits: the Ruby cell runs, then the Go cell is compiled with the type and runs, in the same run. When a later edit changes the type, only the Go cells that read the variable are compiled again.
data.in-the-browser#In the browser: The playground runs Ruby cells too, with no server: the same rbgo and go-scikit bindings, compiled to WebAssembly. The page fetches the Ruby core (playground-ruby.wasm) only when the open notebook has a Ruby cell, so a visitor who runs only Go never downloads it. While the first core downloads, the page shows what go-notebook does, in cards that link to these pages; a core already in the browser’s cache opens the notebook without them. The Ruby there has no bridge to the page’s JavaScript and no file system, and every figure a cell shows goes through an allowlist SVG sanitizer before it reaches the page. Try the Ruby examples on go-notebook’s own playground, go-statistics and go-numerics.
data.limits#Limits:
A notebook is a program, and it runs with your rights. A Ruby cell can reach what a Go cell can: files through File, IO and Dir, other processes through Process, the environment through ENV, and the bindings that write files (DataFrame#write_csv, Plot::Figure#save_svg). The rbgo_core build leaves out the network libraries (socket, net/*, openssl): requiring one raises LoadError. Run only notebooks you trust.
Every cell runs in the worker, a process of its own, so the kernel survives whatever a cell does:
What the cell does What happens runs too long with --timeout 30s, its worker is killed and the cell fails with “stopped: the cell ran longer than 30s”; the next run starts a new worker holds too much memory with --memory 512 (MiB), the garbage collector keeps under the limit as long as it can, then the worker is stopped and the cell fails with “stopped: the cell went over its memory limit” recurses without end Ruby raises SystemStackError, shown with twelve frames asks for an impossible allocation ('x' * 2**62) Ruby raises NoMemoryError calls exit or exit! a SystemExit fails the cell; the worker lives on kills its own process (Process.kill, not on Windows; os.Exit in Go) the cell says so, and the next run restarts the worker Both limits apply to Go and Ruby cells alike and are off by default. The memory limit counts the Go heap, sampled every 20 ms; memory held outside it (a large stack, a mapped file) is bounded only by the operating system.
data.the-rules#The rules:
Ruby cells follow the rules of Go cells: one definition per name, no assignment to another cell’s variable, and a name starting with _ stays in its cell. The names come from rbgo’s own parser: a cell defines the locals it assigns at its top level, and the methods, constants, classes and modules it defines there; it uses the names it reads before assigning them.
The Ruby cells share one interpreter, so their top-level locals persist from cell to cell. Dependencies, caching and re-runs work across the two languages as for Go alone: a Ruby cell runs again only when it, or a cell it reads, changed.
A cell that ends in an expression shows its value: a Plot figure as SVG, anything else as its inspect (an NDArray in NumPy’s form). An exception fails the cell with file:line: message (Class) at the notebook’s line, followed by the backtrace frames in the notebook (twelve at most).
